title: Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease: Mastering TRD & End-Stage PDR
summary: Advanced Diabetic Eye Disease (ADED) represents the sight-threatening zenith of proliferative diabetic retinopathy, characterized by Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD), persistent vitreous hemorrhage, and fibrovascular proliferation. This guide provides a residency-level deep dive into its surgical and clinical management.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Ischemic Cascade
content: 1. Chronic Hyperglycemia → Capillary non-perfusion
2. Retinal Ischemia → Upregulation of VEGF & PEDF imbalance
3. Neovascularization at Disk (NVD) or Elsewhere (NVE)
4. Fibrous scaffolding grows along posterior hyaloid face
5. Vitreous contraction → Tangential & Anteroposterior traction
6. Retinal elevation → Tractional Retinal Detachment

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: NVI/NVA: Check undilated gonioscopy for angle vessels.
Vitreous: Shafer sign (uncommon in pure TRD), vitreous heme.
Membranes: Opaque white fibrovascular fronds along arcades.
Macula: Tractional macular edema or heterotopia.
Periphery: Signs of prior incomplete PRP (skip areas).

sections.title: Urgent Red Flags
content: Rapid vision drop in one eye (Combined TRD/RRD)
Sudden 'curtain' with flashes (New break)
Painful red eye with high IOP (NVG)
Macula-threatening TRD (Urgent surgery indication)
B-scan showing 'kissing choroidals' or total RD

branches: B-Scan Ultrasonography (Critical if VH is dense)
Wide-field FFA: Identify areas of non-perfusion
B-Scan: Look for 'V' or 'X' shaped configuration

rows: Early vs late vitrectomy had similar 2-year outcomes.
Early PPV leads to better VA in very severe cases.

content.explanation: T: TRD involving macula; R: RRD (Combined); A: Acute premacular heme; C: Chronic VH (>3 mo); T: Tight hyaloid; I: Iris neovasc (NVG prophylaxis); O: Opacity preventing PRP; N: Neovascularization progression despite laser.

sections.title: Surgical Management Protocol (PPV)
content: 1. Port Placement: 23G, 25G, or 27G Pars Plana Vitrectomy.
2. Core Vitrectomy: Clear central vitreous hemorrhage.
3. Induction of PVD: Often difficult due to tight adhesions; use Triesence/TA.
4. Segmentation: Cutting membranes into small islands to relieve tangential traction.
5. Delamination: Peeling membranes off the retinal surface using shears or forceps.
6. Hemostasis: Endodiathermy for bleeding fronds; increase IOP temporarily.
7. Endolaser: Complete 360-degree Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP).
8. Tamponade: Air, Gas (SF6/C3F8), or Silicone Oil if breaks are present.

sections.title: Key Surgical Techniques & Tools
content: Bimanual Technique: Using a chandelier light and two instruments.
Viscodissection: Injecting Healon GV to separate membranes.
Foldback Technique: Starting delamination at the edge of a membrane.
Vertical Scissors: Crucial for cutting tight bridges between retina and hyaloid.
Valved Cannulas: Maintain stable IOP during instrument exchange.

sections.title: Post-operative Management
content: Steroid-Antibiotic drops (Pred Forte/Vigamox) QID.
Atropine 1% BD if significant inflammation/gas.
Prone positioning if gas/oil tamponade used.
Monitor IOP closely (risk of steroid response or gas expansion).
Early Anti-VEGF (Avastin) injection if recurrent VH occurs.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Fellow
content: Don't 'chase' every peripheral membrane; focus on relieving macular traction.
Pre-op Anti-VEGF (2-7 days prior) significantly reduces intra-op bleeding.
Always check the renal status; ADED patients often have diabetic nephropathy.
In cases of NVG, perform PRP/PPV early to save the optic nerve.
TRD fluid is slowly absorbed; don't expect immediate flattening post-op.
